family_lesson.where_to_look_first: Ask whether the apparent 'flower' is actually a capitulum. Find the involucre and its phyllaries, then separate the individual florets on the receptacle. Confirm fused anthers around the style, an inferior one-ovule ovary, and a 1-seeded cypsela often crowned by a pappus.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Capitulum of many florets on one receptacle + surrounding involucre of phyllaries + usually 5 syngenesious anthers forming a tube around the style + inferior 1-ovule ovary + cypsela with pappus or pappus reduced/absent.
authoritative_framework: The primary inflorescence is a head/capitulum, not one flower.
The involucre is the complete set of phyllaries surrounding the head.
The receptacle supports the florets and may be paleate, bristly, hairy, pitted or naked.
Corollas are fused and may be tubular, ray-like, ligulate, bilabiate or reduced depending on floret type.
Five anthers are usually united into a cylinder around the style.
The style elongates through the anther tube and often presents/sweeps pollen before the stigmatic surfaces become receptive.
Each fertile floret has an inferior, 1-locular ovary with one ovule.
The fruit is more precisely a cypsela because it develops from an inferior ovary, although 'achene' is common in older botanical treatments.
The pappus represents the calyx and may be bristles, hairs, awns, scales, a crown, or absent.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not call the ray florets petals; each ray is an individual flower.
Do not assume every head has both ray and disk florets.
Do not assume ray florets are always sterile or always fertile; sexuality varies by genus and even within genera such as Coreopsis.
Do not assume disk florets are always bisexual/fertile; Silphium provides a local counterexample with functionally staminate disk florets.
Do not assume every cypsela has a feathery pappus; pappus form varies widely and may be absent.
Do not identify Asteraceae from a daisy-like outline alone; verify phyllaries, individual florets, anther tube and fruit.

terminology_lock.involucre: The collective ring/basket of bracts around the head.
terminology_lock.receptacle: The shared platform bearing the florets.
terminology_lock.palea: A small receptacular bract subtending an individual floret in paleate heads.
terminology_lock.ray_floret: A marginal floret with a strap/ray-like zygomorphic corolla; may be pistillate, sterile, or neuter.
terminology_lock.disk_floret: Usually a central tubular/actinomorphic floret; may be bisexual, functionally staminate, or otherwise specialized.
terminology_lock.ligulate_floret: A 5-toothed strap-shaped bisexual floret characteristic of liguliflorous Cichorieae heads.
terminology_lock.cypsela: The 1-seeded indehiscent fruit produced from the inferior ovary.
terminology_lock.pappus: Modified calyx atop the ovary/cypsela; hairs/bristles/scales/awns/crown or absent.
terminology_lock.synantherous: Anthers united into a tube around the style.

head_type_cards.definition: Outer ray florets plus central disk florets.
head_type_cards.teaching_note: This is the familiar 'daisy/sunflower' appearance, but each apparent petal is a ray floret.

head_type_cards.definition: No ray florets; all florets have roughly actinomorphic tubular corollas.
head_type_cards.teaching_note: Asteraceae does not need to look daisy-like.

head_type_cards.definition: No showy rays; outer pistillate florets are slender/filiform and surround inner tubular bisexual or functionally staminate florets.
head_type_cards.teaching_note: This head contains two floret types even though it looks eradiate.

head_type_cards.definition: All florets ligulate, bisexual and usually fertile; characteristic of tribe Cichorieae.
head_type_cards.local_pool_note: No classic Cichorieae genus is currently among the 28 mapped Asteraceae genera, so use this as a family-breadth comparison rather than a primary local anchor.
head_type_cards.teaching_note: A dandelion-type head is many strap-shaped florets, not one flower with petals.

Radiate head.

exception_cards.lesson: head type can vary even within a familiar genus

Ray florets, when present, are pistillate/fertile.

pollen_presentation_lesson.key_point: The fused anther tube and advancing style are one of the family's best microscopic recognition characters.
sequence: Label anther cylinder around the style.
Show style elongating through the tube and pushing/sweeping pollen upward.
Show bifid style arms opening with stigmatic surfaces.
pollen_presentation_lesson.teaching_value: This explains why Asteraceae looks so different from superficially head-forming families with free anthers.

fruit_pappus_lesson.key_point: Trace one fertile floret from inferior ovary to mature cypsela.
sequence: compare bristly, scaly/awned, reduced and absent pappus forms
fruit_pappus_lesson.caution: Use 'cypsela' in the learner, while noting that many floras still call the same fruit an achene.

fast_key: Apparent flower surrounded by phyllaries -> ask if it is a capitulum of many florets.
Radiate head -> isolate one ray and one disk floret; each is a separate flower.
No rays -> inspect whether head is discoid or disciform rather than abandoning Asteraceae.
Five anthers united into a tube around a bifid style + inferior one-ovule ovary -> very strong Asteraceae confirmation.
Mature 1-seeded cypsela + pappus or pappus scar -> strong reproductive confirmation.
Compound umbel with no involucre/phyllary basket and a 2-part schizocarp -> Apiaceae instead.
Head of many tiny flowers but stamens free and no Asteraceae-style pappus/cypsela -> reconsider non-Asteraceae head-forming families.

Apiaceae.tie_breaker: Apiaceae organizes separate flowers into umbels and matures a 2-part schizocarp. Asteraceae packs florets on a common receptacle inside an involucre and produces 1-seeded cypselae.

Caprifoliaceae_Dipsacaceae_like.tie_breaker: Teasel/scabious-like heads can look composite, but their flowers retain a different calyx/epicalyx architecture and do not have the Asteraceae synantherous anther tube + cypsela/pappus system.

Amaranthaceae.tie_breaker: Papery bracted heads/spikes may look composite, but individual flowers have free stamens and lack the Asteraceae involucre/floret/anther-tube/cypsela package.
